nameStory: The coral hairstreak gets its name from the beautiful coral-red spots that dot the undersides of its wings, resembling tiny jewels against a gray backdrop. Like all hairstreaks, it has delicate thread-like tails extending from its hindwings that look like fine hairs, giving this group of butterflies their distinctive name.
description: The coral hairstreak is a small, delicate butterfly with a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches. Its wings are dark brown to grayish-brown on top, while the undersides reveal the signature coral-red spots that make this species special. Unlike many of its hairstreak relatives, this butterfly lacks the typical white stripes across its wings, making it easier to identify once you know what to look for. The tiny hair-like tails on the hindwings are shorter than those of most other hairstreaks.

idTips.label: Coral-red spots
idTips.description: Look for bright coral or orange-red spots arranged in a row along the undersides of both forewings and hindwings - these spots are distinctive and won't be found on other hairstreaks

idTips.label: Plain gray underside
idTips.description: The wing undersides are smooth gray without the white lines or stripes that mark most other hairstreak species - feels almost powdery if you could touch it

idTips.label: Short tails
idTips.description: The hair-like tails on the hindwings are noticeably shorter and stubbier than those of banded or striped hairstreaks

idTips.label: Dark upperside
idTips.description: When wings are open, they appear uniform dark brown to gray-brown with no obvious markings or blue patches

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About the size of a penny when wings are spread, with a delicate, almost fragile appearance as it flutters around flowers

habitat: Coral hairstreaks prefer open areas with wild cherry trees nearby, including forest edges, old fields, meadows, and power line cuts. They're often found in areas where wild black cherry or choke cherry grows, as these are their caterpillar host plants. Look for adults visiting flowers in sunny clearings and woodland borders throughout New England's hills and valleys.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active - caterpillars are developing inside wild cherry buds and feeding on the emerging leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from mid-June through July when adults are most easily spotted visiting flowers like dogbane, milkweed, and wild bergamot in sunny openings.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished their flight period, but eggs have been laid near cherry buds where they'll overwinter until next spring.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, tucked safely near wild cherry buds, waiting for spring warmth to trigger hatching.

funFact: Coral hairstreak caterpillars are essentially cherry tree specialists that live inside the flower buds and eat them from the inside out - they're so well-camouflaged that you could be looking right at an infested cherry bud and never know a caterpillar is having dinner inside!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other hairstreaks, but the coral hairstreak is actually easier to identify than most because it lacks the white stripes of banded and striped hairstreaks. Memory trick: 'Coral spots, no stripes' - if you see bright coral-red spots on plain gray wings, you've found your coral hairstreak.
compareHints: Among New England's hairstreaks, the coral hairstreak stands out for what it lacks - no white stripes like the banded or striped hairstreaks, and no blue patches like some others. The coral-red spots are unique in the genus, making this actually one of the easier hairstreaks to identify once you learn to look for the distinctive orange-red markings against the plain gray background.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hairstreak relatives, the Banded Hairstreak is distinguished by its prominent white-edged bands across both wings, while Edwards' Hairstreak has more muted markings and Coral Hairstreak lacks tails entirely.
Among the hairstreaks in its genus, Edwards' Hairstreak is most similar to Banded Hairstreak, but Edwards' has more subdued underside markings and is more closely associated with scrub oak habitats.

Among New England's hairstreaks, the striped hairstreak stands out for having the most regular, parallel striping pattern - think of neat ruled lines rather than the zigzag or broken patterns of banded or Edwards' hairstreaks.
Among New England's hairstreaks, the Hickory Hairstreak is most similar to the Banded Hairstreak, but Banded Hairstreaks typically have more distinct banding patterns on their underwings.
Among its hairstreak relatives, the Acadian stands out for its very short upper tail and relatively plain gray underside.
